title: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
gist: Subscription search company Kagi launched Kagi Mail (public beta, web-only) plus a calendar as a paid, privacy-first Gmail alternative priced at $9/month or bundled in the $25 Ultimate plan. The author sees it heading the right way but needing refinement, and the email pitch is harder than search given Proton Mail and Tuta competition.

insights.claim: Kagi Mail launched in public beta as a web-only, ad-free email service with unlimited aliases and domains, 50GB storage, Sieve rule-based filtering, an anti-lock-in data policy, an MCP server and optional off-by-default AI agent features.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Shipping an MCP server signals privacy-focused email vendors positioning for agent-driven inbox access.
insights.locator: The email interface, currently in public beta

insights.claim: Kagi Mail lacks native apps and a contacts address book at launch; the roadmap targets a contacts book in Q1 2027 and Android/iOS apps in Q4 2027.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Missing core features limit near-term adoption; watch roadmap delivery as the gating factor for any switch from Gmail.
insights.locator: Some major features are still missing

insights.claim: Kagi Mail costs $9 per month or $99 per year standalone (60-day trial), is excluded from Kagi's $5 and $10 search plans, and is bundled only in the $25-per-month Kagi Ultimate plan that also includes frontier AI models.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Kagi is using bundling to push users up to its highest-ARPU tier.
insights.locator: Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service

insights.claim: Kagi Search has just over 75,000 paying subscribers, tiny compared with Google Search, Bing or DuckDuckGo user bases.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Paid privacy search remains a niche with no measurable threat to Alphabet's search share.
insights.quote: Kagi Search has just over 75,000 paying subscribers
insights.locator: According to the company, Kagi Search

insights.claim: Kagi's thesis, partly endorsed by several Ars Technica staffers who switched from Google Search to Kagi, is that ad-sales incentives pollute Google's search results and increasingly its email.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Perceived ad-driven quality decay at Google is the core demand driver for paid search alternatives among power users.
insights.locator: Kagi also argues that Google’s search results

insights.claim: The paid-email pitch is harder than paid search because most users do not perceive Google's ad incentives harming Gmail, though Google's aggressive insertion of Gemini into Gmail may be changing that perception.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Aggressive AI integration into Gmail could become a churn catalyst that benefits privacy email providers.
insights.locator: The pitch for email is a little harder

insights.claim: Kagi Mail enters a privacy-email market with established rivals: Proton Mail, the most popular, offers end-to-end encryption but is embroiled in controversies, and Tuta, which Kagi itself praises as a good alternative.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Proton's controversies may open a window for newer privacy-email entrants like Kagi.

insights.claim: After a few hours of use, the author judges Kagi Mail to be heading in the right direction but needing refinement before it could permanently unseat Gmail.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Not yet a credible Gmail substitute for mainstream users; revisit after native apps ship.
insights.quote: it will need refinement to permanently unseat Gmail
